questions.stem: Peter, 39, has consented to a perianal examination in left lateral with the practice nurse chaperoning. When you gently part his buttocks you see a linear split at 6 o'clock. He flinches, and the anal verge is visibly puckered and tight. You had planned a digital rectal examination. What is the best next step in the station?
options: Proceed with DRE using generous lidocaine gel and a slow single-finger insertion
Stop, defer the DRE, explain why to Peter and document it with a plan to re-examine
Pass a lubricated proctoscope to view the anal canal and exclude a second lesion
Ask Peter to bear down so that the full length of the split can be seen
questions.why: A visible fissure with sphincter spasm and severe tenderness is enough for the diagnosis. Forcing a DRE or proctoscopy hurts, makes the spasm worse and adds nothing now. Defer it, tell the patient, document it and re-examine once healed or less tender.
notes: Even with local anaesthetic gel, a DRE in acute fissure is very painful and adds nothing to a diagnosis already visible on inspection.
Proctoscopy is even more painful than a DRE in acute fissure and isn't needed to make the diagnosis; it can wait for review.
Straining doesn't help show a fissure and is uncomfortable. Bearing down is used to show prolapsing haemorrhoids or rectal prolapse.

questions.stem: Peter, 39, returns to his GP after 2 weeks. He has used psyllium, drinks more water and takes warm sitz baths, and his stools are now soft. Every bowel motion is still painful and the posterior midline fissure has not healed. He takes no other medicines. What is the most appropriate next treatment?
options: Paracetamol with codeine 30 mg, up to four times daily for 2 weeks
Refer now for lateral internal sphincterotomy under general anaesthetic
Glyceryl trinitrate 0.2% ointment applied to the anal canal 12-hourly for up to 8 weeks
Hydrocortisone-containing haemorrhoid ointment applied twice daily until healed
questions.why: When conservative care fails, the next step is to relax the sphincter with a topical agent: GTN 0.2% ointment (or diltiazem 2%) to the anal canal every 12 hours for up to 8 weeks. Warn about headache, and it must not be used with PDE5 inhibitors.
notes: Codeine causes constipation and harder stools, which tears the fissure again. It should be avoided in anal fissure.
Sphincterotomy is kept for chronic fissures where topical treatment (and often botulinum toxin) has failed, because it carries a risk of incontinence.
Corticosteroid haemorrhoid preparations don't relax the internal sphincter or help healing, and long-term use thins the anoderm.

questions.stem: Peter, 39, developed a posterior midline anal fissure after passing a hard stool 4 days ago. Each bowel motion is so painful that he now puts off going to the toilet. Which mechanism best explains why the fissure is failing to heal?
options: Internal sphincter hypertonia raises anal pressure and cuts anodermal blood flow
External sphincter spasm obstructs venous drainage of the internal haemorrhoids
Infection of the anal crypt glands spreads into the intersphincteric space
Coeliac-related mucosal atrophy impairs epithelial turnover in the anal canal
questions.why: Pain causes spasm of the internal anal sphincter. The spasm raises resting pressure and reduces blood flow to the posterior anoderm, which is poorly perfused to start with, so the tear becomes ischaemic. Holding on hardens the stool and tears it again. Treatment relaxes the sphincter and softens the stool.
notes: The persistent hypertonia in a fissure is in the internal sphincter (smooth muscle). Venous obstruction is a mechanism for haemorrhoids, not fissures.
Infection of the anal glands is the cryptoglandular mechanism of perianal abscess and fistula, and he has no signs of either.
Coeliac disease affects the small bowel mucosa, not the squamous anoderm of the anal canal, and his disease is controlled on a gluten-free diet.

questions.stem: Peter, 39, has an acute posterior midline anal fissure running from the anal verge into the distal anal canal, below the dentate line. He describes 10/10 sharp, cutting pain with each bowel motion. Which nerves carry this sharp, well-localised pain?
options: Visceral afferents travelling with the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2 to S4)
Sympathetic afferents travelling with the inferior hypogastric plexus
Cutaneous branches of the ilioinguinal nerve (L1)
Inferior rectal (anal) branches of the pudendal nerve (S2 to S4)
questions.why: Below the dentate line the anoderm has somatic innervation from the inferior rectal branches of the pudendal nerve, so lesions there cause sharp, well-localised pain. Above the line the innervation is visceral, which is why internal haemorrhoids are usually painless.
notes: Pelvic splanchnic visceral afferents supply the mucosa above the dentate line and carry only poorly localised, dull sensation.
The inferior hypogastric plexus carries autonomic fibres to the rectum and upper anal canal, not somatic pain from the anoderm.
The ilioinguinal nerve supplies the groin, anterior scrotum and medial thigh, not the anal canal.
